Display Strings In, Raw Numbers Out

occurrences.body:
Agent Roster & Personas

There are exactly two agents, and separately three personas. The agent is who answers; the persona is which voice the second agent wears.

tuntun_ai is the professional investment analyst. It owns the tool pipeline, runs a fixed six-section analysis framework, and is token-streamed to the client.

customer_service_manager is the relationship layer. It runs one-shot on a separate SSE endpoint, receives the already-executed tool result, and is instructed never to contradict the analyst or introduce analysis of its own.

The wire value is customer_service_manager. cs_manager is only code and route shorthand — cs_manager_person, /chat/cs_manager/answer, ENABLE_CS_MANAGER — and never travels in selected_agents.

Personas are Luna (the default whenever settings are nil, empty, or unrecognised), Kevin, and Mia. Each has two embedded prompt files under core/persona/prompts/ — an answer variant and a suggestion variant — selected by call site, not by a heuristic. The persona is frozen per turn as cs_manager_person, so changing your setting never re-labels old messages.

Benefits:

  • One analyst, one relationship layer — no second opinion to reconcile.
  • Persona is a prompt file, not code; adding a fourth is a text file and an enum value.
  • Per-turn persona persistence keeps conversation history historically accurate.
  • Independent failure domains: a customer service manager failure cannot fail an already-streamed analyst turn.

Server-Owned Routing

The LLM does not choose the agent. It emits three understanding booleans; the server owns the truth table and re-derives selected_agents unconditionally. The planning prompt is written to match, and says so out loud: "You do NOT decide which agent(s) respond."

graph TD IN["routing booleans from classify_and_plan"] P{"need_professional_analysis"} Q{"need_personalization OR marketing_opportunity"} A1["customer_service_manager only"] A2["tuntun_ai then customer_service_manager"] A3["tuntun_ai only"] IN --> P P -->|"false"| A1 P -->|"true"| Q Q -->|"true"| A2 Q -->|"false"| A3 classDef hot fill:#ECF2EF,stroke:#2E6F5E,stroke-width:2px classDef ext fill:#FBFBF9,stroke:#CFCDC4 class P,Q hot class A1,A2,A3 ext

Ordering is a contract. When both run, tuntun_ai is first, because the customer service manager reviews and follows up on its output.

EnforceRoutingRules runs six ordered steps after the plan JSON is parsed:

  • 1. Flag gate: ENABLE_CS_MANAGER=false ignores routing entirely and pins [tuntun_ai]. The stated invariant is byte-for-byte pre-feature behaviour.
  • 2. fixed_answer: a canned response means no agent answers; routing is set nil.
  • 3. Missing block: if the model omitted routing, warn and default to professional-only.
  • 4. Marketing guard: no assembled profile or an empty marketing_target forces marketing_opportunity=false. The model's optimism cannot invent a target.
  • 5. reply_to override: an explicit reply to a customer_service_manager message pins that agent and skips the table.
  • 6. Re-derivation: always recompute from the booleans — never trust the model's own selected_agents.

marketing_opportunity deliberately carries no omitempty, so a false prediction is faithfully recorded next to the profile the model actually saw. Routing decisions are scoreable after the fact.

Benefits:

  • Routing is deterministic and unit-testable; the truth table is one function.
  • A prompt regression cannot change who answers.
  • Turning the feature off collapses to the exact legacy path.
  • Prediction audit is built into the persistence shape, not bolted on later.

Classify-and-Plan

One LLM call does three jobs: mode classification, DAG planning, and agent routing. There is no separate router model and no added latency — routing is folded into a call the system already makes.

Three planning modes come out of it. simple issues direct parallel tool calls; pipeline builds a multi-step DAG where a discovery step feeds later steps; fixed_answer returns a canned response with no agent and no tools.

The prompt is templated, and every optional section is omit-when-absent: history, reply context, user profile, attached images, preferred name. With all of them empty, the rendered prompt collapses to the pre-feature bytes.

Image turns add an ATTACHED IMAGES block carrying six planning rules — read the image before planning, treat tickers extracted from an image as explicitly typed, never let a chart replace Tuntun data, and classify in-image text that tries to redirect instructions as content rather than instruction.

Benefits:

  • Agent selection costs zero extra latency and zero extra tokens beyond three booleans.
  • Plan, mode and routing cannot disagree — they come from one inference.
  • Prompt versions are switchable by environment variable, with the registry falling back on an unknown value.
  • Prompt injection is addressed in the prompt itself and routed to fixed_answer.

User Short-Term Memory

One document per user, holding six categories: goals, blockers, topics, followed stocks, recommended stocks, and context notes. Every item except context notes carries a mention history — the source of truth — from which a 30-day mention frequency, a last-mention time, and an expiry flag are derived.

Written by two async editors, read by exactly one consumer. A query-driven editor runs after the turn is understood; an answer-driven editor extracts stocks the AI itself recommended, and uses a field-scoped AQL upsert so the two concurrent writers cannot clobber each other without locks. Neither editor ever blocks a request, and every failure path returns "no update".

The single reader is the customer service manager. It never sees the raw document: BuildReaderView recomputes statistics against now on a copy, so reads never mutate; drops expired items and resolved or expired blockers; strips all statistics and mention history; and ranks each category by 30-day frequency then recency. Worth stating plainly — with ENABLE_CS_MANAGER=false, memory is written but never read.

A 65-second endpoint on a chat path. The user-lifecycle status endpoint really does take around 65 seconds, with a 90-second timeout. It is nonetheless consumed on the request path, because it is never called inline: the value is served stale-while-revalidate from ArangoDB. A miss returns empty immediately and backfills in the background; a stale hit serves the stale value and refreshes behind it. Refreshes are deduplicated by a package-global single-flight refresh guard — it deduplicates concurrent refreshes of one cached value, so two subsystems cannot both fire the 65-second call — and run panic-guarded on a detached context with a dial timeout matched to the budget.

The governing rule is deliberate: on an ArangoDB read error, do not refresh. There is no point launching a 65-second call whose result could not be persisted anyway. An absent status renders as an empty string, so the prompt section vanishes rather than carrying a placeholder.

Benefits:

  • Memory quality improves without ever adding latency to a turn.
  • The reader gets a ranked, decayed projection instead of raw storage.
  • A very slow upstream dependency is consumed safely on a live chat path.
  • Two concurrent writers, one document, no locks.

Evidence-Based Memory Editing

The memory editor is prompted against its own worst instinct. Existing items are framed as a "reference dictionary, NOT a checklist to copy", and the model is forbidden from emitting any derived statistic field — frequencies and expiry are backend-computed.

Lifecycle status is evidence only. The prompt states it must never by itself create a goal, blocker, topic, followed stock, or context note. It exists solely to justify flipping an existing blocker to RESOLVED — objective proof, not a source of new memory.

The model structurally cannot write EXPIRED. A normaliser collapses anything that is not OPEN or RESOLVED down to OPEN. Expiry is backend-only: the system independently flips stale-but-unresolved blockers. That gives three keys to closing a blocker — explicit user confirmation, objective lifecycle proof, or time — and the model holds only one of them.

Merge semantics are additive with no deletes. Canonical keys are case-insensitive trimmed strings, matches record a mention, misses append. Items leave only via 30-day expiry or capacity eviction. Context notes are the single full-replace category, and only when the model explicitly sets context_notes_update, so a structured-only turn cannot wipe them.

Cost is gated too: the answer-driven editor runs a cheap pre-filter — a standalone four-uppercase-letter IDX ticker shape, or one of twelve bilingual recommendation keywords — before it will spend an LLM call, and defers its database read until the model confirms a recommendation.

Benefits:

  • Memory cannot be inflated by a system signal the user never mentioned.
  • State transitions the model should not own are made unrepresentable, not merely discouraged.
  • Additive merging makes accidental data loss a capacity decision, not a model decision.
  • Non-recommendation answers skip the LLM call entirely.

Seam-Marker Prompt Composition

Persona files are plain English. They keep literal tokens — {{AI Answer}}, {{User Short Term Memory}}, {{User Profile}} — whose embedded spaces make them invalid Go template fields, and they delimit optional spans with HTML comments such as <!-- USTM_START --> and <!-- USER_PROFILE_START -->.

Rendering is therefore not text/template. The builder does line-based span stripping followed by a strings.Replacer pass. Leftover tokens with no value to substitute are neutralised into ordinary section references — "the AI Answer section below" — so no raw token and no delimiter comment ever reaches the model, and a blank-line collapse tidies what stripping leaves behind.

The point is authorship. A persona is a character sheet a non-engineer can edit: no template syntax to break, no build step, and a missing value removes a whole section cleanly rather than leaving an empty header.

Benefits:

  • Prompt authors edit readable English, not template expressions.
  • A malformed token degrades to prose instead of failing the render.
  • Optional sections disappear entirely, keeping token counts honest.
  • The same seam markers make the flag-off render provably identical to pre-feature.

Image Upload Pipeline

Images arrive as multipart parts on POST /v2/chat/submit, alongside a JSON payload part. A body cap is applied before the multipart parse, sized as files-per-query times per-file limit plus a megabyte of headroom. Each part is read behind a bounded reader, so an oversize upload is detected without ever being buffered whole.

Validation never trusts the client. Not the declared Content-Type, not the filename extension — only sniffed bytes. HEIC is probed explicitly by ISO-BMFF ftyp brand across ten brands, because the standard library reports application/octet-stream for all of them and iOS uploads would otherwise be rejected. Other ISO-BMFF brands deliberately fall through, so a video cannot pass as an image. An empty allow-list rejects everything: a misparsed configuration fails closed, never open.

Limits are three files per query, 20 MB each, image/jpeg, image/png, image/heic. IDs are img_ plus twelve hex characters from crypto/rand, so ownership is not the only defence.

Persistence never gates answering. The synchronous step does no I/O at all. Persistence is detached and builds its own 30-second context, because the 202 response cancels the request context. Failures are logged, never returned — a disk problem degrades to "the answer still streams, the image just is not downloadable later".

Benefits:

  • Oversize and malformed uploads are rejected without buffering or touching disk.
  • Storage failures cannot fail a turn.
  • Blob-then-metadata ordering with rollback makes orphan blobs unrepresentable.
  • Persisted ids are read from the same context the model read, so history cannot claim an image the model never saw.

Kind-Agnostic File Assets

Everything below the ingestion handler is kind-generic. The blob store, the metadata store, the download handler, and the id grammar know nothing about images. All kind-specific knowledge lives in two maps: id prefixes, and the validator policy handed to the service.

On-disk layout is <root>/<kind>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<id>.<ext>, UTC-sharded so directories stay small and a future TTL sweep is a directory operation. Directories are 0700, files 0600. Writes go to a temp file in the destination directory and are renamed into place, with cleanup on every error path, so a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated blob under an id that metadata already references.

Metadata lives in an Arango file_assets collection with a unique hash index on file_id — the backstop behind random id minting — plus persistent indexes for per-request resolution and per-owner sweeps. Writes use a create, not an upsert: a duplicate id must be a loud error, because silently overwriting would hand one user's id to another user's bytes.

Two id checks exist and they are not interchangeable. One classifies by prefix only and is documented as accepting img_../../etc/passwd; the other enforces the full grammar. Anything that touches a store or a path must use the second.

Voice is scaffolding only. The kinds and id prefixes exist, storage collapses the streaming variant onto voice, audio extensions are already mapped, and the download handler is per-kind gated. But both voice kinds are hardcoded disabled, there is no voice configuration flag, no /voice/stream socket, no voice route, no registered voice validator, and no speech-to-text. Voice does not ship today; what shipped is the shape it will land into.

Benefits:

  • Adding a modality is a kind plus a policy entry, not a new subsystem.
  • Atomic writes and restrictive permissions by default.
  • Traversal-shaped ids are rejected before any store call.
  • Dark kinds return 404 without revealing that they exist.

Dual Multimodal Transport

Two wire formats, because two clients are in play.

Data URIs, for the langchaingo path. The application reaches Gemini through an OpenAI-compatible client, and langchaingo marshals llms.BinaryContent into a shape no OpenAI-compatible endpoint understands. Only llms.ImageURLContent carrying a base64 data: URI serialises to the accepted image_url form. A test asserts the emitted JSON, so this cannot be "simplified" back into a broken state.

Native inline data, for web_search. That tool sits on the native SDK, so it emits real inline_data parts with raw bytes and no base64 inflation.

Five multimodal call sites:

  • The planner — images on the human message only, since provider support for images in a system message is inconsistent.
  • The simple-mode streamer — switches to a content-generation call with a streaming callback, because the string-only streaming API cannot carry parts. The text-only path stays untouched.
  • compare_stocks synthesis — every construction of the message pair goes through one helper, so the degraded-data path cannot silently drop image parts.
  • web_search grounding — native inline data, with a conditional system-prompt block appended only for image turns.
  • The customer service manager — added after the agent answered "I don't have the image in front of me" to the most common conversational image question.

Pixels never go into prompts. A text summary carries only the count, the ids, and the ordering, so a prompt can say "the second chart" and the model can resolve it. Embedding base64 in a text section would roughly double the per-image token cost. Every site reaches the attachments through the one canonical gate; four duplicated copies of that flag-check were deliberately collapsed into it.

Benefits:

  • One documented wire format per client, asserted by tests rather than by comment.
  • Token cost stays linear in images, not doubled by base64 in text.
  • A single gate means the flag flip lands everywhere at once.
  • Text-only turns keep their original, cheaper code path.

Attachment Cache Fingerprinting

The cache key was question text plus language. That is a correctness hole the moment images exist: "what does this chart say?" with an image would hit the entry cached for the same sentence without one, and return an image-blind answer.

The fix is a fingerprint over content, not ids. SHA-256 across each blob, length-prefixed and in order, truncated to sixteen hex characters and appended as :img_<fp> after the language suffix. Length-prefixing keeps two different splits of the same bytes distinct; ordering makes a swapped pair a different key. Hashing content rather than the minted id means the same screenshot legitimately shares an entry.

Three independent bypass guards then keep image turns off the cache entirely:

  • Routing — an image-bearing turn skips the cache fast-lane and goes straight to the queue.
  • Read — the cached-request handler returns early before obtaining a Redis client, so no round trip is issued at all. This covers both entry points and any future third caller.
  • Write — one ShouldCache field gates both the Redis write and the cache-populated notification, which also closes the promotion path: a key that was never notified can never be matched.

Three reasons are recorded for the bypass. A cache hit rebuilds the log row inside the fast lane without image ids, so replaying would silently drop them from history. An image-only turn has an empty question, collapsing the key until the digest is the sole discriminator. And a 64-bit digest is realistically never hit twice, so the entry is pure Redis bloat.

Benefits:

  • An image turn can never be answered from a text-only cache entry.
  • Both key segments stay independently greppable.
  • With the flag off, keys are byte-identical to pre-feature — nothing already cached is invalidated.
  • Guards are independent, so no single missed branch re-opens the hole.

Dark-Launch Flag Discipline

ENABLE_IMAGE_PROCESSING defaults to false, and the off-path contract is written down verbatim next to the flag: parts read past and discarded, no cache fingerprint, prompts text-only, no file_assets documents, image ids absent everywhere, download endpoint 404.

The interesting part is that the contract is mechanically proven, not claimed. Building a multimodal message with no attachments is byte-for-byte identical to the plain text-parts constructor. Building search contents with no images is exactly the plain text query. And twelve pinned prompt goldens are checked in and asserted, so a prompt change surfaces as a reviewable diff — regenerating them requires an explicit flag.

Earlier guards compared the render against HEAD, which silently accepted any regression the moment it was committed. Checked-in goldens do not.

The same discipline runs through the multi-agent work: ENABLE_CS_MANAGER=false pins routing to the single agent, removes the routing section from the planning prompt, skips profile assembly, and collapses dispatch to the legacy single call. Every optional prompt section — routing, profile, memory, reply context, images, preferred name — disappears entirely when absent rather than rendering an empty placeholder.

The download route exists while dark and returns 404, so flipping the flag needs no redeploy and a dark deployment reveals nothing about what is coming.

Benefits:

  • Features ship to production disabled, with the disabled path under test.
  • "No behaviour change" is an assertion in CI, not a reviewer's judgement.
  • Enabling is a configuration change, not a deployment.
  • Prompt drift is visible as a diff before it reaches a model.

The Three-Layer Lock

A condition the user stated out loud is locked, and the lock is a flag test, never a language test. There is no Locked boolean on the domain type: origin = user_explicit is the lock. Nothing re-reads the sentence to decide.

origin = user_explicit"] R{"toolpicker.RelaxationCandidates"} EX["Excluded from the auto-relax set
layer 1"] P["Planner changed it anyway"] A{"baseline.Authorize
Span, or RelaxRequest.Target == CID"} OK["Change kept
explicit_relax_by_name"] REV["Change reverted
planner_violation, layer 2"] AUD["observe R1 drift audit
scores both halves, layer 3"] C --> R R --> EX C --> P P --> A A -->|"authorized"| OK A -->|"not authorized"| REV OK --> AUD REV --> AUD classDef hot fill:#ECF2EF,stroke:#2E6F5E,stroke-width:2px classDef ext fill:#FBFBF9,stroke:#CFCDC4 class R,A hot class OK,REV,EX ext

Layer 1 — exclusion. toolpicker.RelaxationCandidates leaves every user_explicit condition out of the auto-relax candidate set, so the relaxation engine cannot reach it at all.

Layer 2 — authorization. baseline.Authorize compares the planner's condition list against the baseline, reverts any unauthorized change to a locked condition, and records a planner_violation. There are exactly two authorization signals, and deliberately no third: the condition's own Span, and a RelaxRequest whose Target matches the CID.

Layer 3 — the audit. The daily drift audit in observe needs both halves of the evidence: the negative (planner_violation) and the positive (explicit_relax_by_name). Score only the negative and every legitimate user-requested loosen becomes a false P1. The engine writes both from one function, so neither can be wired up without the other.

Sacrifice order composes with the lock rather than duplicating it. Each Origin also carries a relaxation rank — constraint_default 0 < preset_default 1 < inferred 2 < user_explicit 3 — and the lowest is given up first. A new Origin value falls to the default arm and is therefore held longest: an unclassified origin must never inherit "give this up first" by accident, and TestEveryOriginHasADistinctRelaxationRank fails until someone classifies it deliberately.

Benefits:

  • The lock cannot be defeated by phrasing, because phrasing is never consulted.
  • A planner regression surfaces as a reverted change plus an audit row, not as a silently loosened filter.
  • The drift audit measures both directions, so it does not punish the behaviour it wants.
  • Adding an Origin fails a test until its sacrifice order is stated.

Ladders, Never Invented Numbers

Numbers in this tool come from exactly two places: the user types one, or the registry supplies a ladder step. Nothing else may produce one. RelaxedParams being non-nil is the relaxability gate for a condition, and every value in it must be a step on that filter's ladder — so relaxation walks a ladder it was handed rather than guessing a looser bound.

The rule used to have an exception, and the exception was deleted, not deferred. An earlier design let the system propose a looser threshold and ask the user to confirm it; the whole mechanism was removed on the reasoning that a proposal saves the user nothing — both paths cost two turns — while forcing the system to invent the very number the rule forbids. Gone entirely: suggestions, expected_hits, pending_written, PendingConfirmation and its session slot, confirms_pending, explicit_relax_suggested, explicit_relax_confirmed, and the suggest-then-confirm state machine that tied them together.

Deleting it made the lock stricter. The system now never touches a locked condition at all — not even by proposing a value for one.

What replaced it carries two facts and no proposal: the near-miss report names which condition is blocking (n_dropped) and the value actually reachable on that metric. Both are read off a sensitivity matrix execute has already paid for, so the report costs nothing extra.

Benefits:

  • No threshold on screen is ever a model's guess — it is the user's or the registry's.
  • One fewer state machine, one fewer session slot, and one fewer way to drift.
  • The near-miss report is derived from data already in hand, not from a second query.
  • The rule is checkable: a number with no ladder step behind it is a bug, not a judgement call.

Content Is the Routing; the Label Only Lies

One design principle runs through the whole tool: content is the routing; the label only lies. When a field's content and the planner's own label disagree, the code trusts the content and logs the mismatch.

It shows up first at the tool boundary. The caller must pass the user's message close to verbatim in demand_description, because fuzzy Indonesian terms — murah, bagus, bandar, likuid — have to survive intact for the tool's own planner to resolve them against the lexicon. A caller that helpfully normalises the sentence destroys the signal before the only component that could use it.

The LLM-facing tool description carries two routing rules in bold, both written against observed misrouting. A combination of criteria is always this tool, never stock_ranks — that is the trap, because a single-criterion request genuinely does look like a ranking table. And criteria may arrive as Pine-Script-style code, a formula, or a checklist, not only as a sentence.

Inside the turn the same principle governs turn_mode. It is the only multi-turn signal the code trusts from the planner, and all it does is select which baseline this turn builds on. What actually changed is derived by diffing the full condition list against that baseline — never reported by the model.

Benefits:

  • A mislabelled turn still produces the right screen, because the label is not load-bearing.
  • Fuzzy natural-language terms reach the one component that can resolve them.
  • The misrouting trap is documented where the router reads it, not in a wiki.
  • Label and content mismatches are logged, so prompt drift is measurable.

Four Turn Modes, One Diff

TurnMode has four values and one job: choose the condition list this turn builds on.

  • continue — build on the previous turn's list.
  • fresh — start from an empty baseline.
  • next_batch — the baseline is the stored list verbatim, and the model's own conditions field is ignored outright.
  • handback — not a picking request at all.

Everything downstream is derived. baseline.Diff compares the planner's full condition list against the selected baseline; the lock runs on that diff; constraint derivation runs deliberately after the lock, so a system-derived constraint can never be mistaken for something the user said.

Identity is two-level by design. CID (c1, c2 and so on) is within-turn and model-supplied; CondKey is cross-turn and derived in code by DeriveCondKey. The model never gets to name a condition across turns.

Provenance is recorded, never inferred. Normalization merges an auto-added bound into the user's own condition object, so SystemAddedKeys exists to say which keys the system put there. The type's own comment is blunt about it: do not infer provenance from the value — a minValue of zero does not mean system-added, because a user can legitimately state a zero floor.

A next_batch turn is usually not a query at all. A lineage row-set cache with a short TTL (STOCK_PICKER_RESULT_CACHE_TTL, default five minutes) makes the next page a local slice rather than a re-query, and sessions live 24 hours.

Benefits:

  • One enum carries the whole multi-turn contract; everything else is computed.
  • Paging is cheap, because the next page is a slice of a result already held.
  • Cross-turn identity is code-owned, so a model-renamed condition cannot orphan its history.
  • Provenance survives the merge that would otherwise erase it.

The Lexicon & the Registry

"Murah" is not a number, and engineers are not the right people to decide what it means. The lexicon package owns the schema and the loader; the content belongs to the product manager, held as JSON and uploaded through POST /stock_picker/lexicon/overwrite. That endpoint always uses static auth, deliberately ignoring DYNAMIC_AUTH.

Two expansions run off it. A preset turns one fuzzy word into a set of conditions. A constraint adds an implicit bound a human would assume but nobody typed — a liquidity floor under a value screen, say. Both are tagged at birth: preset output carries origin = preset_default, constraint output constraint_default, and those origins are exactly what make them the first things relaxation sacrifices.

The ordering is deliberate. Preset expansion runs before the lock; constraint derivation runs after it. A preset is part of what the user asked for and must be diffed; a constraint is the system's own addition and must never enter the diff as if it were the user's.

Underneath sits the capability registry — 98 filters across 11 groups, generated from the screener's own get-all-indicator response and refreshed hourly, with a hand-authored overlay supplying what the API does not carry: each filter's polarity and its relaxation ladder. The filter identifier is the API's indicatorTag verbatim, so there is no translation table to drift.

Benefits:

  • The meaning of a vague word is a product decision, editable without a deploy.
  • Generated-plus-overlay keeps the registry honest about which half is vendor truth.
  • Origin tagging makes "give this up first" fall out of where a condition came from.
  • No translation table between the domain model and the API means no drift to debug.

Relaxation & the Near-Miss Exit

A screen that returns nothing is a failure of the product, not of the user. relax runs three strategies in a fixed order and proposes nothing of its own.

Single-point first: loosen one condition by one ladder step and recount. Then cumulative greedy: keep loosening, cheapest first, where cheapest is one comparator built from Priority — larger means more important, so the smallest is sacrificed first — composed with the origin's relaxation rank. Locked user_explicit conditions are not in the candidate set at any point, so neither strategy can reach them.

If nothing reachable remains, the near-miss exit ends the turn with two facts and no proposal: which condition is blocking, and the value actually reachable on that metric. Both come from the sensitivity matrix already computed, so the exit costs no extra call.

The guard beside it matters as much. A fresh screen that arrives with zero conditions to screen on exits as clarify:no_conditions — a clarification, explicitly not a tool_error. Asking the user a question is a normal outcome here, not a failure, and the logs keep the two apart.

Benefits:

  • An empty result set becomes an explanation instead of a dead end.
  • Relaxation order is one comparator, so it is testable and stable.
  • Every loosened value is a ladder step, so the result stays defensible to a user.
  • "Ask a question" and "something broke" stay distinguishable in the logs.

Measured Before Integrating

The screener runs on top of a separate filter API. Before a line of integration code was written, a standalone probe exercised that API end to end and captured every response to disk. The integration was then designed against those captures, and six of its properties are load-bearing enough that the client is built around them:

  • Transport is JSON. application/x-www-form-urlencoded is rejected outright.
  • The indicator catalogue is fetched with POST, not GET.
  • The envelope carries data, errorCode and message, so HTTP 200 is not success — a business error arrives as 200 with an errorCode other than FS000000. The client reads the body, never the status line.
  • The catalogue is 98 filters across 11 groups, and that response is exactly what the capability registry is generated from.
  • No server paging, no server sort, no count-only mode. Eight paging and sort parameter spellings were sent and silently ignored; a single response simply carries every match.
  • Responses are human-formatted display strings while requests take raw numbers.

Two further measurements shaped the design. No authentication is required — 2046 matches came back with no user id and no token. And a broad query is expensive enough to budget for: 611ms for 2046 rows and 223KB at concurrency 1, rising to 2547ms and 2.1MB at concurrency 9. That cost is precisely why the sensitivity matrix is recomputed locally from one response instead of asking the API the same question 2N+1 times.

execute is the only package in the tree permitted to speak to this API, so every one of these six properties is handled in exactly one place.

Benefits:

  • The integration was designed against captured responses rather than assumptions.
  • Those captures double as fixtures, so a change on the far side surfaces as a failing test rather than a production mystery.
  • One package owns the API, so a seventh surprise has exactly one place to land.
  • Latency budgets rest on numbers someone actually observed.

One Loose Query, the Whole Matrix

The expensive question a screener asks is "how many would match if I moved this one bound?" — once per condition, in each direction, plus the strict count. That is 2N+1 queries against an API with no count-only mode, where every count costs a full payload.

The measured API makes the obvious version unnecessary. One response carries every match, with one value column per filter requested. So issue a single loose query — the conditions with their bounds widened — and the entire 2N+1 sensitivity matrix can be recounted locally from that one response. No second call.

It is treated as an optimisation, not as doctrine. The local recount was verified exactly against the server once — 478 against 478 — then shipped behind an interface with a per-variant-call fallback and a boundary-condition suite. The evidence is filed as encouraging, not proven — one exact match is a good sign, not a proof, and the fallback exists precisely because of that distinction.

The matrix is built lazily, so a turn that returns plenty of results never pays for it. Relaxation and the near-miss report are both readers of the matrix, which is why neither of them costs a round trip.

Benefits:

  • Sensitivity analysis collapses from 2N+1 network calls to one.
  • The fallback keeps the per-variant path alive, so the optimisation can be switched off.
  • Laziness means the common, successful turn pays nothing for it.
  • The confidence level is recorded honestly rather than rounded up to "proven".

Display Strings In, Raw Numbers Out

The screener API is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is a factor of 1012. Requests take raw numbers: a 50 trillion rupiah market-cap floor is sent as 50000000000000. Responses come back as human-formatted display strings — "204.44T", "5,050", "-65.99%".

Confusing the two is not a rounding error, it is a twelve-order-of-magnitude error, and it bit the measurement probe itself twice before the contract was written down.

So the rule is positional rather than clever: execute performs the conversion in exactly three places and nowhere else. Every other package in the tree works in raw numbers only and never sees a display string. A fourth conversion site anywhere is the bug.

The same instinct governs storage. The per-turn audit row embeds the planner output, the conditions, the sensitivity map, the relaxation steps, the near-miss report, the result rows, the disclosures and the reachable outcome directly — which is exactly why the root package's own documentation says a JSON tag change there is a storage-format change, not a refactor.

Benefits:

  • A whole class of silent magnitude bug is confined to three reviewable lines.
  • Domain code never has to ask which representation it is holding.
  • The three-places rule is auditable by grep, not by discipline.
  • The storage contract is stated where someone editing a struct tag will read it.

The Import DAG

Three import cycles appeared independently while the feature was being built — baseline against relax, toolpicker against lexicon, toolpicker against ragpick. One rule resolved all three at once, and it is now the shape of the tree.

Every subpackage imports toolpicker, the root. The root holds types, constants and pure helpers only — no behaviour. No subpackage imports another except in the direction stated. And nothing imports engine: engine is the single orchestrator, the only subpackage permitted to import every other, and the only thing the tool registry imports.

The rule buys properties that are hard to retrofit. baseline — the lock, the diff, normalization — has no database, LLM, clock or goroutine in any exported function, so the most security-sensitive logic in the feature is also the most trivially testable. observe is the only picker package that touches db. serve is the only place allowed to construct a payload. execute is the only package that speaks to the screener API.

The root's own cost is stated plainly: because the audit row embeds root types directly, types.go is a persisted wire contract, and a JSON tag change there is a storage-format change.

Benefits:

  • Three cycles were closed by one rule instead of three workarounds.
  • Pure packages need no fixtures, so the lock is covered by ordinary unit tests.
  • Each capability has exactly one owner, so "where does this happen?" has one answer.
  • The orchestrator reads top to bottom, because nothing calls back into it.

A Payload, Not an Answer

stock_picker ends by handing back a structured payload — totals, condition views, the relaxation trace, disclosures, data_as_of and risk notes — and the pipeline's LLM writes the sentence the user reads.

That the tool could have written the answer is the interesting part. An answer package exists, carrying an answer prompt and the compliance copy registries, and it has no production caller. engine does not import it at all. Calling it inside the tool would produce a finished answer as a tool result, which the pipeline LLM would then be asked to answer from: two models writing the same paragraph, the second paraphrasing the first.

Persistence is the last thing the turn does, not the first thing it forgets. Every exit path — a handback, a clarification, a near-miss, a successful screen — writes its row to ai_stock_picker_turns before the tool returns. The row embeds the planner output and the full derived state, so a turn can be reconstructed exactly.

Fourteen stages run in a fixed order per turn, and the schema the calling LLM sees is a single required string, demand_description. Everything above is derived from that one field.

Benefits:

  • One voice answers the user; the tool contributes facts, not prose.
  • The payload is renderable by a non-LLM client too, because it is structured.
  • Persist-before-return means no completed turn is unexplainable after the fact.
  • A one-field schema gives the calling planner nothing to get wrong.

Runtime Kill Switch

Two different mechanisms gate this tool and they are not interchangeable.

The ENABLE_STOCK_PICKER family is boot-time. ENABLE_STOCK_PICKER is unusual among the project's flags in that it gates registration rather than callability — off, the tool is not in the registry and the planner never sees its schema. DISABLED_TOOLS remains an independent kill switch on top of it. ENABLE_STOCK_PICKER_SIMILAR, ENABLE_STOCK_PICKER_RISK_FLAGS and ENABLE_STOCK_PICKER_AUDIT_JOB gate the branches: with the similar branch off the turn tail is byte-identical to its shape before that branch existed, and with risk flags off the resolver is a no-op and the risk notes stay empty.

The incident switch is something else entirely: a control-plane document in ai_stock_picker_flags, read by observe on every invocation and cached 30 seconds. Flipping it stops the tool within half a minute, with no redeploy and no restart. Collection bootstrap is deliberately not gated on ENABLE_STOCK_PICKER, so a flag flip on a deployment that has never run the tool still finds its collections.

Around it, observe is the single event API for the feature: it writes the audit row, scores seven guardrails daily, and raises four realtime rate alerts to DingTalk. The deployment status today: ENABLE_STOCK_PICKER=true is pinned in both the production and staging compose files, and stock_picker has been live in production since 2026-09-23.

Benefits:

  • An incident is a flag flip measured in seconds, not a deploy measured in minutes.
  • Boot flags keep a dark path genuinely dark — no schema, no tool, no surface.
  • Bootstrapping outside the flag means enabling never meets a missing collection.
  • Guardrail scoring and alerting live with the event API that already sees every turn.

What Was Not Built

Three capabilities were designed in full and deliberately not built. Saying so out loud is part of the design.

The RAG-picking branch. It has no package. When the planner emits a rag_request, the branch is left nil rather than faked — the turn does not pretend to have run a retrieval it never ran.

The second similarity engine. The similar-stock side branch ships one engine; a second, retrieval-based comparables engine was designed and deliberately not built. The engine that did ship has five distinct exits and carries its lineage across next_batch turns, so paging a similarity result behaves like paging a screen.

The answer package. Built and tested, with no production caller, for the reason given under "A Payload, Not an Answer": the pipeline LLM writes the answer.

The same precision governs what is built. The risk-flag resolver handles the 17 IDX Notasi Khusus codes and is explicitly not an UMA resolver — an AST test fails the build on any identifier that claims otherwise. The feed is one whole-market fetch on a refresh schedule, held in memory with the last good value served on failure, so the answer path's ResolveFlags is a map read under a read lock with no reachable network call.

Benefits:

  • An unbuilt branch returns nil, so nothing downstream mistakes it for an empty result.
  • The gap between the plan set and the shipped tree is written down, not inferred.
  • A test, not a convention, stops the risk-flag resolver from drifting into UMA.
  • Risk annotation adds no latency and no new failure mode to the answer path.

Cache Fast-Lane

Every text-only submit is offered to the cache fast-lane before it is allowed near the FIFO queue. dispatchForProcessing pushes the request onto cacheRequestChan with a 10 ms bound; if that channel is full the request falls through to the queue. Three dedicated goroutines (TOTAL_CACHE_WORKERS, default 3) drain the channel. They never acquire processingSemaphore, so a cache hit costs nothing from the normal worker budget.

The key is built exactly once per submit, in helpers.GenerateCacheKeyWithHistory — the single place in the system where cache keys are generated. It concatenates the previous questions and the current question, normalises the result to lowercase letters and digits only (Unicode-aware, so Chinese survives), and prefixes it. A :lang suffix is appended when a language is set, and :img_<fp> when the turn carries image attachments, where the fingerprint is the first 16 hex characters of a SHA-256 over each blob, length-prefixed.

conversation_id is deliberately excluded from the key. Two people asking the same question in two different conversations land on the same entry. That exclusion is the whole point: it is what turns a per-conversation cache into a cross-conversation, cross-user duplicate-work collapser.

Cache Promotion & Re-evaluation

The up-front cache check only helps a request that arrives after an answer exists. Promotion covers the other case: a twin that missed the cache and is already sitting in the FIFO queue when the first request finishes computing.

The loop has five steps, all on the write side of the streamer:

  • Write. RedisResponseCache.Store marshals the response, selected tools, completion status, detected language and sources, sets the key with a 24 h TTL, and then verifies the write before anything else happens.
  • Notify. Streamer.Stream calls NotifyCachePopulated(cacheKey), a non-blocking send onto a buffered channel. A full channel is logged and dropped — the notification is an optimisation, never a correctness requirement.
  • Re-evaluate. A single ReevaluationWorker goroutine consumes cache keys and calls PromoteFromQueueForCache.
  • Promote. queue.Manager.PromoteForCache looks up every queued request sharing that key in O(1) through cacheKeyIndexMap. For each one it sends the request id to priorityChan first, and only on a successful send removes the item from the FIFO and stashes it in promotedItems. If the priority channel is full the request simply stays in the queue. No orphans, and no window in which a normal worker can race in and regenerate it.
  • Serve. priorityRequestWorker picks the id up and tries HandleCachedRequestViaReevaluation before anything else. Because the write was verified before the notification fired, the answer is already durably in Redis. Only a genuine miss — the entry evicted or expired between write and pickup — falls back to regeneration.

Promoted turns complete with status completed_from_cache_reevaluation rather than completed_from_cache, chosen from the promotion flag and deliberately ignoring whatever status was cached. The two timescales stay distinguishable in the logs.

Benefits:

  • N identical concurrent questions cost one plan, one tool run and one synthesis. The rest are replayed from Redis.
  • PromoteForCache is the only queue-jumping edge in the system. There are no priority classes and no other path that reorders the FIFO.
  • Send-then-remove ordering makes promotion safe under a full priority channel: the worst case is that the request processes normally.
  • Promotion serves from the cache rather than the LLM, so a queue-jump costs a Redis read, not a model call.

Plan-and-Execute Pipeline

The orchestration core is a custom implementation of the plan-and-execute / LLMCompiler pattern. One LLM call in tools/toolcore/planner emits the entire execution graph as JSON up front; a deterministic engine in tools/toolcore/pipeline then runs it. It is not a ReAct loop — the model does not observe a tool result and pick the next tool.

The planner classifies each turn into one of three plan modes: simple (independent tools, no dependencies), pipeline (ordered steps where later steps consume earlier output), and fixed_answer (a canned response, for example on prompt-injection detection). Simple mode is not a second code path — plan.ToPipelinePlan() converts it into a one-step pipeline so everything flows through the same executor.

Within a step the execution mode is single or map. Single runs the step's tools in order; map runs one tool once per item of an upstream array, normally the stock codes a generator step produced. The runtime switch also accepts parallel and treats the LLM's occasional simple step-level value as an alias for it. A separate per-step boolean, AggregationMode, marks a terminal step that executes no tools and instead concatenates every prior step's output for the synthesising LLM.

The interesting part is what happens after the model returns. An LLM's JSON is never trustworthy enough to execute directly, so the plan runs a deterministic repair gauntlet: argument-shape normalisation, the iron rule that step 1 of a real pipeline must be a stock-code generator (otherwise the plan is rewritten into aggregation mode), demotion of bogus pipelines back to simple mode when the declared dependencies do not exist, and correction of map-parallelism and direct-stream flags the model set wrong.

Why this is not LangChain, LangGraph or Eino:

  • Across Eino, Genkit-Go, trpc-agent-go and LangChainGo, the DAG is always author-defined in Go at compile time. Nothing in Go executes an LLM-emitted DAG off the shelf. Even LangGraph's LLMCompiler is a tutorial pattern you assemble yourself.
  • The repair layer and the domain resolver — JSONPath over step outputs, {{code}} substitution per map iteration, sector and rank tagging — encode Tuntun's tools and financial rules. No framework ships them. They stay ours under any choice.
  • So the real trade is "own a small execution substrate too" versus "bolt the unavoidable custom layer onto someone else's pre-1.0 API". Eino is v0.9.x, LangChainGo v0.1.x.
  • LangGraph matches the pattern but means returning to Python, which this codebase left for documented GIL reasons. langchaingo is already a dependency, used for exactly the right thing: a multi-provider LLM client, not orchestration.

Full reasoning, with line references: docs/architectures/custom_pipeline_vs_frameworks.md.

Parallel Map Execution

A map step runs one tool once per item of an upstream array — typically the stock codes a generator step produced, capped at 30 by default. Run serially that is 30 sequential backend calls. ExecuteToolsMap instead fans out over a bounded worker pool: a buffered channel of size ParallelLimit acts as the semaphore, one goroutine per item takes a slot, and a sync.WaitGroup joins them. Each result carries its index and is written into a pre-sized slice, so the joined output stays ordered regardless of completion order, and a failed iteration becomes a failure marker rather than failing the whole step.

The limit is per step. ExecuteToolsMap reads step.ParallelLimit and falls back to config.AppSettings.DefaultParallelLimit when the planner left it unset — DEFAULT_PARALLEL_LIMIT, default 5, raised to 20 in the development .env. Each individual tool call is retried through the shared retry helper at DEFAULT_RETRY_LIMIT (default 3) with exponential backoff from 1 s, capped at 30 s.

FIFO Queue & Processing Semaphore

Admission control is deliberately plain. queue.Manager is a slice-backed FIFO with two index maps for O(1) lookup and removal. EnqueueNewRequest rejects with ErrQueueFull at QUEUE_SIZE (default 100), then does a non-blocking wakeup send onto a signal channel — the channel carries a nudge, not the payload. DequeueRequest takes index 0. That is the entire scheduling policy: fairness is plain arrival order.

Concurrency is capped by two semaphores at different stages:

  • processingSemaphore, sized MAX_CONCURRENT_REQUESTS (default 50), acquired in processRequest and released when the task hands off. The normal worker pool is also sized to the same number, so the semaphore is the real ceiling on in-flight processing.
  • llmStreamSemaphore, sized MAX_CONCURRENT_LLM_STREAMS (default 5), held by runBoundedStream for the whole stream. The preparer stage hands a stream off and moves on, so without this leash a burst of prepared requests would spawn unbounded concurrent streams and push the provider into 429s, which trips the circuit breaker.

The development .env raises two of these: QUEUE_SIZE=1000 and MAX_CONCURRENT_LLM_STREAMS=30. MAX_CONCURRENT_REQUESTS is left at its default of 50. Two channels bypass the queue entirely — the cache fast-lane workers, which never take processingSemaphore, and the priority workers that serve cache-promoted requests.

A janitor runs every JANITOR_INTERVAL (2 m) and reaps three classes of stuck request: cancelled but never picked up (1 s), queued past QUEUE_TIMEOUT (1 h), and processing past PROCESSING_TIMEOUT (10 m).

Benefits:

  • One queue, one policy. No priority classes, no scan-and-select, nothing to reason about beyond arrival order.
  • Separating the processing cap from the LLM-stream cap lets planning proceed at width 50 while only 5 streams talk to the provider.
  • Rejecting at QUEUE_SIZE gives the client a fast 503 instead of an unbounded wait.
  • The janitor bounds the blast radius of anything that gets stuck, without any per-request timer.

Stateful Conversations

History is fetched once per turn, at submit time, not during preparation. helpers.FetchAndFormatHistory (chatbot/helpers/history.go) takes the last HISTORY_ITEMS turns — default 1, set to 3 in the development .env — via arangoStore.GetConversationHistory(ctx, conversationID, limit). When the caller supplies prev_context on the request, that is used instead and the database is not touched at all.

It is called from helpers.GenerateCacheKeyWithHistory, so a single call produces both things the turn needs: the formatted transcript and the list of previous question strings that feed the cache key. The result travels on types.CacheKeyData for the rest of the request's life — into PreparedRequestData.FormattedHistory, into the planner's PlanOnly call, and into the final synthesis prompt.

The default rendering is one line pair per turn:

Human: What is the market cap of BBCA?
Assistant: BBCA's market capitalisation is ...
Human: What about BBRI?
Assistant: ...

Turns that were answered by both agents render with role labels instead — Tuntun AI: and CS Manager: — so the customer-service agent can recognise its own prior turns. That branch only fires when the split output fields are non-empty, which happens under ENABLE_CS_MANAGER; older rows take the legacy path and render byte-for-byte as before. Either way the extracted question list is unchanged, so the cache key is unaffected by the transcript format.

Benefits:

  • Follow-up questions ("what about BBRI?") resolve against the previous turn.
  • One fetch serves both the prompt and the cache key — no second read, and no chance of the two disagreeing.
  • prev_context lets a caller supply history directly and skip the database round trip.
  • Failures degrade to empty history rather than failing the turn.

At the traffic this service actually sees, that threshold is not reached, so the breakers are dormant in practice and do not trip. Benefits:

  • Failing fast beats holding worker slots open against a dead dependency — once the threshold is reachable.
  • Error classification stops ordinary "not found" results from being read as an outage.
  • Recovery is automatic: a cooldown, then a bounded number of probes.
  • Every state transition is logged, so a trip is visible in log aggregation.

Service Discovery with Self-Healing Cache

Most backend endpoints are configured as service URLs rather than hosts: 34 of the BE_* settings use the form consul://service-name/path (auth, feed-static-service, feedhistoryservice, value-investing-web, sector-concept-web, funds-service, and others). toolutils.ResolveServiceURL turns that into an http://host:port/path before any HTTP client sees it, because http.Client cannot dial a consul:// scheme. A non-consul URL is returned untouched, so mixed configuration works.

Retries. Consul is intermittently unreliable, and a service being redeployed produces a momentary window with no healthy instances. Neither should fail a user's request. The health query runs inside utils.RetryWithDelay, bounded by CONSUL_RESOLVE_MAX_ATTEMPTS (default 3) with CONSUL_RESOLVE_RETRY_DELAY between attempts (default 1s). Both a query error and an empty healthy-instance list are retryable. Exhausting the attempts emits a single caller-agnostic log line tagged event=consul_resolution_failed, so every failed resolution is findable regardless of which tool triggered it.

Cache. A process-local map holds the chosen host:port per service until CONSUL_RESOLVE_CACHE_TTL expires (default 1h). Only the host and port are cached, keyed by service name — never the full URL — so one entry serves every path on that service. Setting the TTL to zero or below disables caching entirely. Live resolutions log at INFO with event=consul_resolved_live, which makes cache effectiveness directly measurable: more than one per service per TTL means the cache is not doing its job.

Self-healing. A cached address can go stale — the instance dies, Consul knows, this process does not. InvalidateService evicts the entry for a service, and callers invoke it on failure. The auth client is the live example: on a transient ErrAuthUnavailable it evicts the entry before its next retry, so the retry re-resolves against Consul instead of hammering a dead address.

Benefits:

  • Backend instances can move without a config change or a redeploy.
  • A redeploy window on a dependency does not surface as a user-visible failure.
  • Consul is queried at most once per service per TTL instead of once per tool call.
  • A dead cached address is corrected by the first request that trips over it.

Stale-While-Revalidate Reads

The user-lifecycle-status endpoint takes roughly 65 seconds to answer. Its configured budget, BE_USER_LIFECYCLE_STATUS_TIMEOUT, is 90 s. It nonetheless feeds a chat turn, because the lifecycle tag is evidence for memory editing and for the marketing funnel. lifecyclecache.Cache.Fetch resolves this by never calling it inline.

Every read is a single ArangoDB point read against the user_lifecycle_status collection:

  • Fresh hit — serve the stored value.
  • Stale hit (older than USER_LIFECYCLE_STATUS_TTL, 24h) — serve the stale value anyway, and spawn a background refresh.
  • Miss — return empty immediately, spawn a refresh to backfill. The prompt section simply vanishes rather than carrying a placeholder.
  • Arango read error — return empty and deliberately do not refresh. There is no point launching a 65 s call whose result could not be persisted.

Refresh discipline. refreshAsync is single-flighted per user through a package-global sync.Map, shared by every Cache instance, so the memory editor and the profile assembler cannot both fire the slow call for the same user. To be precise about what that deduplicates: it collapses concurrent refreshes of one cached value, not user requests — the requests themselves were already served from the cache and never waited. The goroutine is panic-guarded, detached onto context.Background() so it outlives the triggering request, and builds a cloned transport with DialContext set to the same budget, so an unreachable backend fails at the configured 90 s rather than at the default transport's dial timeout. The raw response body is persisted verbatim, so backend schema drift needs no migration.

The same shape guards authentication. When CACHE_VALID_CREDENTIALS is on, a successfully validated dynamic-auth credential is stored in Redis under two windows: VALID_CREDENTIAL_TTL (1h) is the freshness boundary, VALID_CREDENTIAL_STALE_TTL (24h) is the actual key TTL. Inside the fresh window the auth service is not contacted at all. Past it, the credential is revalidated — and the outcome matters: a definitive rejection evicts the entry and rejects the request, but if the auth service is merely unavailable the stale credential is served within the grace window. A Redis failure fails open to remote validation. An auth outage therefore degrades to "recently seen users keep working" instead of locking everyone out.

Benefits:

  • A 65-second dependency sits on a chat path without adding measurable latency.
  • Concurrent consumers of one user's lifecycle value trigger exactly one refresh.
  • Nothing is refreshed that could not be stored, so a database outage does not become a stampede on the backend.
  • An auth-service outage does not log out active users.

State-Aware Janitors

Two independent background sweepers keep in-memory state from accumulating. They cover different maps with different rules.

1. Request janitor

A ticker on JANITOR_INTERVAL (default 2m) walks activeRequests and applies a timeout chosen by the request's current state, because "stuck" means something different in each:

  • StateCancelled — CLIENT_PICKUP_TIMEOUT, default 1s. The cancellation packet has been emitted; if the client has not collected it almost immediately, the slot is reclaimed.
  • StateQueued — QUEUE_TIMEOUT, default 1h. Waiting in a busy FIFO is normal behaviour, not a fault.
  • StateTaskExecution and StateFastLaneProcessing — PROCESSING_TIMEOUT, default 10m. Long enough for a real multi-step pipeline, short enough to kill a genuinely wedged one.

The scan reads every holder field under the read lock and captures the pointer, so the cleanup phase needs no second lookup that could race. A timed-out request gets an error pushed onto its error channel, then CleanupRequest.

2. Bowl janitor

A separate 5-minute ticker inside chatbot/bowl drops expired bowls and their request metadata. Expiry is also state-aware: a completed or cancelled bowl expires 30 s after completion — the grace window that lets a resume fired right at the end still succeed — while a still-active bowl is given twice the 24 h TTL. Completion additionally runs the sweep synchronously, so the frontend's auto-resume loop does not find a bowl that has already finished.

Shutdown. Manager.Shutdown closes the async log queue first and waits up to 10 s for the log writer to drain before stopping the cache workers, the cache re-evaluation worker and the bowl manager. Pending chat-log writes are flushed rather than dropped on exit.

Benefits:

  • No unbounded growth in activeRequests or the bowl map.
  • A patient queued request is never mistaken for a stuck one.
  • The resume grace window is respected instead of being cleaned out from under a reconnecting client.
  • Graceful shutdown does not lose queued log rows.

Ordering is the interesting part. The state is written to cancelled before cancelFunc() is called. A client disconnect is not a cancel. The SSE handler says so explicitly. Because the purge removed the request from the map cancellation relies on, a later resume re-registers it, otherwise the resumed-but-still-running turn would answer 404 to a genuine cancel.

Benefits:

  • A stop actually stops the tools and the LLM call, not just the SSE writer.
  • Cancelled turns are recorded as cancelled, never as errors.
  • The partial answer the user already read is preserved.
  • Closing a tab costs nothing and loses nothing — it stays resumable.

Per-User Usage Limits

chatbot/usage is a small tracker over a daily per-user counter in ArangoDB. NewConfig reads four knobs: DAILY_USAGE_LIMIT (default 50), USAGE_TRACKING_ENABLED (default true), and the retry count and base delay used by the increment path.

Admission. CheckLimit runs in the submit handler, before the request is registered or dispatched — a blocked turn costs one point read and nothing else. It compares today's count against the limit and returns whether it is exceeded.

An exceeded limit is not an error. The handler answers HTTP 200 with the standard success envelope carrying status: "usage_limit_exceeded" alongside the request and conversation ids, rather than a 4xx. Quota is a normal, expected state of a chat session, and the client renders it as a message in the conversation instead of as a failed HTTP call — a 429 would land in the same generic error handling as a network fault.

Fail-open. If the counter cannot be read — Arango unreachable, breaker open — CheckLimit logs the error and returns "not exceeded", allowing the request through. A metering failure must not become an outage; over-serving a few turns is strictly preferable to refusing everyone.

Increment is off the hot path. The counter is raised by IncrementUsageAsync after the stream has run to completion, in a fire-and-forget goroutine on a detached 30 s context. It retries with backoff and then fails silently — the user's answer is never delayed or failed by bookkeeping.

Benefits:

  • Cost exposure per user is bounded without any per-request coordination.
  • The rejection is cheap: one read, before any planning, tools or LLM call.
  • Quota exhaustion reaches the client as a first-class state, not an HTTP error.
  • A database problem degrades to unmetered service rather than a hard block.

Context-Aware Caching

Finished answers are cached in Redis under a key built once per turn by GenerateCacheKeyWithHistory — the only place in the system that mints one. The key is the normalised question text plus recent history, a language suffix, and nothing else: ai_chatbot_conv:<simplified>:<lang>. Conversation id is deliberately excluded, so the same question from two users shares one entry. TTL is 24 hours.

Sharing entries is only safe if live data never enters one. Two env lists mark the tools that make a turn uncacheable: TIMEBOUND_TOOLS (deployed as realtime_market,get_current_time) and USERBOUND_TOOLS (the per-user memory, portfolio and watchlist tools). After planning, the preparer runs checkTimeboundToolsInPlanJSON over the generated plan and sets TimeboundToolsCalled. It also sets ShouldCache, via shouldCacheTurn.

The write gate ANDs both. RedisResponseCache.ShouldCache stores only when data.ShouldCache is true, a Redis client exists, TimeboundToolsCalled is false, and the response is non-empty. A skip logs each of the four conditions, so "why was this not cached" is one log line rather than an investigation.

Image turns are excluded by the same field plus two independent guards. Routing skips the cache fast-lane entirely for a turn carrying attachments; the fast-lane read returns before it would obtain a Redis client, so no round trip is issued at all; and ShouldCache being false closes both the Redis write and the cache-populated notification that the promotion path keys on. The cache key also carries a content fingerprint of the attachments, so an image question can never collide with the same sentence asked without one.

Benefits:

  • Live market data is never served from a stale entry, and freshness is configuration, not code.
  • One key generator means the read side and the write side cannot disagree about what a turn is.
  • Excluding conversation id makes the cache genuinely cross-user rather than per-thread.
  • Three independent image guards: any one of them alone is sufficient.

Summarisation Cache

Separate from the response cache, and much narrower. When a comparison pipeline's collected tool output exceeds the token budget, each oversized output is summarised by an LLM call. Those summaries are cached in Redis under summary:<sha256>, with a 24 hour TTL.

The digest is taken over the tool inputs — tool name, marshalled arguments, and whether extreme-reduction mode is active — not over the output text. Identical tool calls therefore share a summary even when the upstream response varies in whitespace or ordering. The stored value keeps the summary, the original and summarised token counts, the reduction percentage, and the time it was cached, so a cache hit still reports honest metrics into the pipeline's LLM-call ledger rather than a zero-cost gap.

USE_SUMMARIZATION_CACHE gates it by passing a nil Redis client, not by branching. prepare.go sets the client to nil when the flag is off, and GetLLMSummary takes the cached path only when its client is non-nil. There is one code path, exercised identically in both modes. The other caller of the summariser, the aggregation fallback in tools/toolcore/executor, simply never supplies a client — so it is uncached by construction, with no flag to get wrong. Timebound and userbound tools are excluded from the cache here too, via the same lists the response cache uses.

It is not request deduplication. A hit skips exactly one summarisation call inside a turn that is already running; it never returns an answer, never short-circuits a request, and does not coordinate concurrent turns. Two identical requests arriving before either has written the entry will both summarise.

Benefits:

  • Repeated comparisons over the same instruments skip the most expensive non-answer LLM calls.
  • Keying on inputs makes hits reproducible instead of dependent on byte-identical tool output.
  • Nil-client gating means the disabled path is the same path, so the flag cannot introduce a behavioural fork.
  • Cached results still carry token and reduction figures, so cost accounting stays complete.

File Asset Integrity

Uploaded bytes are treated as hostile. Neither the client's declared Content-Type nor the filename extension is ever trusted or persisted: SniffMIME reads the leading bytes, probing for the ISO-BMFF ftyp box and its ten HEIF brands first — the standard library reports application/octet-stream for all of them, so iPhone uploads would otherwise be unclassifiable — then falling back to the stdlib sniffer. Other ISO-BMFF brands such as MP4 deliberately fall through, so a video cannot present itself as an image. The allow-list fails closed: an empty list rejects everything, because a misparsed IMAGE_ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES must not silently become "accept anything". A PNG-named file with an executable header is a clean 400.

Ids are minted from crypto/rand: a kind prefix plus six random bytes as twelve lowercase hex characters, so img_ ids are unguessable and ownership checking is not the only defence. A separate grammar check, not a prefix check, guards anything that touches a store, so a traversal-shaped id is rejected by construction rather than by a lookup happening to fail.

Automated Schema & Indexing

There is no migration step to forget. On startup initializeSchema runs ensureAllCollections and then ensureAllIndexes; every call is an idempotent Ensure..., so a fresh database, a restored backup and a running production instance all converge on the same schema. Collections are created unconditionally — including file_assets while image processing is still dark — because gating schema on a runtime flag is exactly how a flag flip returns 500s against a collection that does not exist yet. An empty collection is inert.

Several indexes are correctness constraints as much as query accelerators. Uniqueness on the chat log's request_id, on file_assets.file_id and on a research report's stock_code turns a duplicate into a loud write error rather than a silent overwrite.

Chat logs

  • idx_log_request_id — unique hash on request_id; the lookup behind status, sources and feedback.
  • idx_log_user_conv_time — persistent on user_id, conversation_id, user_query_timestamp; conversation history in order.
  • idx_log_user_session_sort — persistent on user_id, session_sort_ts, user_query_timestamp; backs the session-list query.

Sessions, research, portfolio, memory

  • idx_sessions_user_id — hash on user_id.
  • idx_research_stock_code — unique hash; one equity research report per instrument.
  • idx_portfolio_perm_user_id — unique hash on the portfolio access permission collection.
  • idx_user_memory_user_id — unique hash; one memory document per user.

File assets

  • idx_file_assets_file_id — unique hash; the backstop behind random id minting.
  • idx_file_assets_request_id — persistent; resolve every asset attached to one turn.
  • idx_file_assets_user_created — persistent on user_id, created_at; ownership sweeps and future retention jobs.

Caches and suggestion questions

  • idx_concept_cache_query — unique hash on the cached query string; idx_concept_data_cache_id — persistent on the sector id.
  • idx_all_questions_en — unique hash on the English text, which is how question deduplication is enforced.

Benefits:

  • Deployment is start the binary; there is no separate migration to run or to skip.
  • Named indexes make an unexpected collection scan attributable to a specific missing entry.
  • Unique indexes encode invariants in the database, not only in Go.
  • Schema is flag-independent, so enabling a feature never requires a schema change first.

Asynchronous Chat Logging

The moment a request is accepted, an initial chat-log row is queued rather than written. logQueue is a buffered channel of 100 LogDataForDB values; submitRequest sends on it inside a select with a default branch, so the send never blocks. A single asyncLogWorker goroutine ranges over the channel and performs the write.

The back-pressure behaviour is a drop, and it is deliberate. If the buffer is full the log is discarded with a warning and the request proceeds — the row is a resume and observability aid, not the answer, and blocking the accept path on a database write would be the worse failure. Because the queue has a single consumer, writes stay in submission order. Nothing else uses the queue: the later lifecycle writes, including the final answer, go through CreateOrUpdateChatLog directly on the processing goroutine, after the tokens have already been delivered to the client.

Two details make the deferral safe. The worker writes with context.Background(), so a request the user cancelled a millisecond after submitting still gets its row. And before writing it reads the current completion status: if the row already carries a terminal cancelled or errored... state, written by an earlier status update, the queued "submitted" row would clobber it — so the worker skips the write and instead backfills only the owner and identity fields, which the ownership check on the status endpoint needs in order not to reject the caller forever.

Shutdown closes the queue and waits on a wait group for the worker to drain, with a 10 second bound; a timeout is logged as "some logs may be lost" rather than hidden.

Benefits:

  • A database write is removed from the accept path, so submit latency does not track database latency.
  • Drop-on-full degrades observability under load instead of degrading the service.
  • A background context means cancellation cannot lose the record of the request that was cancelled.
  • The terminal-status check stops an in-flight queued row from resurrecting a finished request.

Structured Turn Records

One turn is one document, created or updated in place on request_id as the request progresses — queued, planned, streamed, finalised. It is not a response log; it is the full execution record, and it is what the status, history, sources and feedback endpoints all read.

Identity and content. Conversation, request and user ids; the user query and the preserved original_message; the assembled final input and the final output; the detected language; the model identity in llm; is_event with its event metadata; any user reaction and feedback with their timestamps. Dual-agent turns store per-agent prompts and outputs in separate fields alongside selected_agents and the resolved persona, leaving the legacy fields untouched when the feature is off. image_file_ids carries the attachments of that turn, in the order the client sent them, read from the same request context the model was grounded on — so the persisted ids cannot disagree with the pixels that were actually sent.

Tool metadata. selected_tools maps a tool name to a list of executions, because the same tool is legitimately called more than once in a turn. Each entry holds the input arguments, the full output text and its token count, the execution duration, a timestamp, the assigned source_number, and, on failure, the error plus the raw provider error body — captured below the client, because the LLM library discards provider detail when the error shape does not match what it expects. Backend tools record the external API address, request payload and response body; multi-API tools record one entry per call. Tools that make their own LLM calls record their input, output, total and grounding token counts.

Timing and tokens. Completion status is a specific value, not a boolean — completed, completed_from_cache, completed_via_pipeline_direct_stream, cancelled, errored_planning, and a dozen more, each naming the path taken. Alongside it: time to first token and the model-only portion of it, plan generation and final answer generation durations, the tools phase wall clock, and a pre-pipeline breakdown down to session setup, cache key generation, queue wait, semaphore wait, language detection and memory access. Token counts are stored per segment — prompt template, tool input, tool output, chat history, completion — rather than as one total. The footnote sources map and the original LLM-generated plan are stored with them.

Cached replays carry the same shape. A cache entry stores the response together with the tool metadata, completion status, time to first token, detected language and sources of the original run, so a fast-lane answer presents the same execution detail as a freshly generated one instead of arriving as a bare string.

Benefits:

  • Latency regressions are attributable to a stage, because every stage is a stored field.
  • A failed turn keeps the provider's own error text, which is usually the only thing that explains it.
  • Per-segment token counts make cost analysis a query rather than a reconstruction.
  • Named completion statuses distinguish the several different ways a turn can legitimately succeed.

Logging is zerolog throughout: 218 non-test Go files import it. logging.Init() runs first in main(), reads LOG_LEVEL (default INFO), and picks a writer from GIN_MODE — JSON to stdout under release, a pretty console writer otherwise. One line is emitted per HTTP request by AccessLog(), registered as the outermost middleware so it records the final status even when an earlier middleware aborts. Beyond the request line, each turn persists a detailed record to ArangoDB. LogDataForDB carries a time-to-first-token decomposition — queue_wait_duration_sec, semaphore_wait_duration_sec, cache_key_generation_duration_sec, language_detection_duration_sec, db_status_check_duration_sec, pre_pipeline_plan_generation_duration_sec, time_to_first_token_llm_service_only, plus an ordered time_to_first_token_breakdown array. Per-tool telemetry lands in pipeline_metrics as ToolExecutionDetail: input args, output token count, duration_sec, retry attempts, cache-hit flag, and the raw external API request and response bodies via api_address/api_input/api_output or an external_apis list for multi-call tools.

Provider errors are captured rather than swallowed. langchaingo discards error bodies whose shape it does not recognise — notably Gemini's OpenAI-compatible 429 — so the raw body is intercepted below the client and stored as llm_error_detail. Failures during streaming are persisted too, through a read-merge-write upsert that records the error and completion status without clobbering fields already written.

Benefits:

  • A single request is traceable end to end by request_id, across the access line, the pipeline logs and the stored turn record.
  • Latency regressions can be attributed to a specific stage rather than guessed at.
  • Rate limits and upstream 5xx keep their original provider text, so triage does not depend on reproducing the failure.
