One wire divergence worth knowing. The Go constant is StateQueued but its serialised value is "submitted", not "queued". Clients must match on "submitted". It is also the fallback: stageToState maps any unrecognised stage string to submitted.

The full set of RequestState values (types/enums.go): submitted, choosing_tools, calling_tools, formulating_final_answer, ready_to_stream, fastlane_processing, cs_manager_generating, completed, cancelled, errored. IsTerminal() is true only for the last three. Two further constants exist but are not status-endpoint values in practice: not_selected is an SSE info signal, and task_execution is declared and read but never assigned outside tests.

What the progress object actually contains. ProgressInfo reports stage, stage_start_time, completion_ratio, and the name lists tools_selected and tools_completed. The ratio advances per pipeline step — it is computed as (stepNum - 1) / totalSteps — not per individual tool, so a step running several tools moves the bar once. estimated_eta_seconds is declared on the struct and copied defensively, but nothing in the codebase ever sets it, so it is omitted from responses. selected_agents is present on /v2 only.

Resolution order is in-memory active requests, then bowl progress when USE_BOWL=true (this is what makes a status poll survive a dropped SSE connection), then ArangoDB with is_from_database: true and a completion_ratio of 1.0. Two races are handled by retry: a 2 s wait at 100 ms intervals for async logging to land, and a 3 s re-check at 200 ms when the database says cancelled. Exhausting all three sources returns 404 NOT_FOUND.

The v1 path deliberately pins the legacy shape: cs_manager_generating is rewritten to formulating_final_answer and progress.selected_agents is stripped. The progress struct is copied before this rewrite because the bowl path returns a live shared pointer.

Benefits:

  • Existing v1 clients see no new states even as the dual-agent path ships behind its flag.
  • A client that loses its stream can recover state from the bowl instead of restarting the turn.

Alerting with Deduplication

common/alert/ pushes operational failures to a DingTalk group webhook. It is three files: dingtalk.go (transport), dedup.go (spam control), manager.go (global wiring and message formatting). The whole subsystem is inert unless DINGTALK_ALERT_ENABLED=true and DINGTALK_WEBHOOK_TOKEN is non-empty — Initialize returns early inside a sync.Once, leaving the global client nil. The default is off.

The webhook client signs each request: HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp + "\n" + secret keyed with the secret, base64-encoded and URL-escaped, with a 10 s HTTP timeout.

The dedup algorithm. An ErrorSignature carries message, error type, model, function, request id and code location — but the bucket key is a SHA-256 of the error type alone. This is deliberately coarse: every RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED collapses into one bucket no matter which tool, model or request produced it. Each bucket then applies, in order:

  • Fresh window — if the current window has expired, the alert always passes and the window restarts.
  • Cooldown — ALERT_COOLDOWN_SECONDS, default 30. Suppressed if the last alert of this type was more recent.
  • Per-window cap — ALERT_MAX_PER_WINDOW, default 1. Suppressed once the bucket has spent its budget.
  • Window length — ALERT_WINDOW_MINUTES, default 60.

Suppression is not silent. Every suppressed alert records its request_id in a set, so one request that retries and trips the same error ten times counts once. The first alert of the next window carries that distinct-request count in its body: "N other request(s) hit a X error and were suppressed in the previous window". A background ticker prunes buckets untouched for two window lengths every 10 minutes.

The message itself carries timestamp, request id, function, model, error type, the error string, and a CodeLocation such as tools/toolcore/planner/planner.go:252 (ClassifyAndPlan), plus optional user query, tool query, user id and prompt preview from the context map.

Benefits:

  • An incident produces one actionable alert per error type per hour instead of a pager storm.
  • The representative alert still reports true blast radius, so coarse bucketing does not hide scale.
  • Defaults are off — a fresh checkout cannot page anyone by accident.

Prompt Versioning & Golden Tests

Prompts are selected at runtime by version string, not edited in place. Four independent knobs exist in config/config.go: PROMPT_VERSION (default v1) for the final answer prompt, CLASSIFY_AND_PLAN_PROMPT_VERSION (default v2) for the planner, SUGGESTION_QUESTIONS_PROMPT_VERSION (default v1), and WEB_SEARCH_PROMPT_VERSION (default v2). Each indexes a template map at call time, so rolling a prompt back is an environment change rather than a deploy of different code. All four are echoed in the startup configuration summary.

The versions are pinned by golden fixtures. core/testdata/flagoff_golden/ holds the rendered final-answer prompt for v1 through v7 plus the comparison prompt, and tools/tooltypes/testdata/flagoff_golden/ holds classify_and_plan_v1 and v2. The tests render each version and assert byte-for-byte equality with its fixture.

The point is not prompt quality — it is proving a feature flag is inert. With ENABLE_IMAGE_PROCESSING off, TestFinalPromptRender_FlagOffMatchesPinnedBaseline and TestClassifyAndPlanRender_FlagOffMatchesPinnedBaseline demonstrate that the prompt the model receives is byte-identical to the pre-feature prompt. Separate ..._FlagOnMatchesPinnedBaseline and ..._ImagesSectionAppearsWhenSet fixtures pin the flag-on rendering, so the on-path is guarded too rather than left unasserted.

Goldens regenerate only under an explicit flag: go test ./core/ -run FlagOff -update-golden. That matters because an earlier version of these tests diffed against git show HEAD: and therefore silently blessed any regression that had already been committed. Requiring the flag forces a prompt change to land as a reviewable diff in the fixture file.

Benefits:

  • Accidental whitespace or ordering drift in a prompt fails CI instead of quietly changing model behaviour.
  • A dark feature is provably invisible to the model while it is off.
  • Intentional prompt changes are reviewed as a diff, by a human, in the pull request.

Dark-Launch Feature Flags

Substantial features ship disabled. ENABLE_IMAGE_PROCESSING (multimodal upload and vision), ENABLE_CS_MANAGER (the dual-agent Luna/Kevin/Mia framework) and ENABLE_USER_SHORT_TERM_MEMORY all default to false. USE_BOWL defaults to true and gates resume. DYNAMIC_AUTH and PRODUCTION_MODE default to false, which together decide whether per-user identity exists at all and whether the mockPass development backdoor is accepted.

The discipline is: gate at the edge, then prove the off-path is unchanged. Flags are checked at the boundary where new data would first enter — request binding, cache-key composition, prompt rendering, history formatting — rather than sprinkled through the core. With ENABLE_IMAGE_PROCESSING off, extractImageAttachments returns silently ignored parts, so a multipart submit from a new client degrades to the old text behaviour instead of erroring.

Tests then assert the disabled path byte-for-byte, not merely "still works": TestCacheKey_FlagOffShapeUnchanged, TestFetchAndFormatHistory_FlagOffByteForByte, TestExtractImageAttachments_FlagOff, TestBuildSearchContents_FlagOffIgnoresContext, TestResolveInterruption_FlagOff_Noop, TestSubmitGate_V2_ImageOnlyRejectedWhenFlagOff, plus the pinned prompt goldens. DYNAMIC_AUTH gets the same treatment through TestAuthStorage_DynamicAuthDisabled and TestHandleSubmitRequest_AuthStorageDisabled.

The operational caveat. Routes are registered unconditionally so a flag can be flipped without a redeploy, which means a dark endpoint answers rather than 404s at the router — with its own code:

  • GET /chat/resume/:request_id — 404 RESUME_DISABLED when USE_BOWL=false.
  • GET /user/settings/:user_id and POST /user/settings — 403 ENDPOINT_DISABLED when ENABLE_CS_MANAGER=false.
  • GET /files/image/:image_file_id — a plain 404 NOT_FOUND when ENABLE_IMAGE_PROCESSING=false, indistinguishable from a missing file, so a prober learns nothing from the dark route.

Clients must therefore treat these codes as "feature unavailable", not as "resource gone" or "you are forbidden".

Benefits:

  • Incomplete work merges to the mainline instead of ageing on a branch.
  • Enabling or reverting a feature is an environment variable, not a rollback.
  • The off-path has test evidence, so "the flag is off" is a verified claim rather than an assumption.
